compression.title: Have I Been Trained?
compression.lede: is a service of Spawning described in 2026 as a free search of the LAION-5B image dataset for whether images trained models such as Stable Diffusion, beside a Do Not Train registry; on 1 November 2026 its pages served a maintenance notice.

sentences.text: Have I Been Trained? (haveibeentrained.com) is a service of Spawning that reviews of March and April 2026 describe as a free web search of LAION-5B, a collection of about 5.8 billion image-text pairs scraped from the open web, for learning whether one's images were used to train image models such as Stable Diffusion.
LAION-5B was the primary training dataset of Stable Diffusion 1.x and 2.x, and the service is a search and detection tool for that one dataset.
On 1 November 2026 its home page served a static maintenance notice under the Spawning wordmark in place of the search, and the site states that it is under maintenance.

Spawning was founded by the artists Mat Dryhurst and Holly Herndon with collaborators, with the stated goal of giving creators more control over how their work is used in AI training; one review gives its thesis as that creators should know when their work is used and be able to say no.

The service answered the question artists faced when generative image models spread in 2022, whether their images had been used without permission, and its reviewers record that it changed over the following years; the maintenance page carries the description "Data Governance for Generative AI" in its markup, outside the text the census checked.

A search takes text, such as a name or a description of a style, or an uploaded image, and returns matching or similar images from the dataset; it runs on OpenAI's CLIP model, which turns the query into an embedding and finds its nearest neighbours in LAION-5B, without pixel matching.
Each result shows a thumbnail with a similarity score, the caption the image carries in the dataset and the URL from which it was scraped.
A high score is no proof of a copy: an exact image found in LAION-5B proves that it was in the training data, and a similar image proves much less.
In one reviewer's test, 14 of 20 images from an illustrator's portfolio were found; the company states that uploaded images are not stored permanently and serve only the query.

Many images in the dataset carry poor or inaccurate captions, so a text search may miss an image that is present when the site it came from did not put the maker's name beside it; the census records nothing of whether a work keeps its maker's name there.

The search covers LAION-5B alone: none of the text-based training data of the language models behind ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, and none of the proprietary image data of Midjourney or OpenAI, which no public tool can search.

LAION-5B is itself a snapshot, compiled mainly from Common Crawl in 2021 and 2022, and the search finds only original images, never a derivative made in a maker's style; not finding a work shows only that it is not in LAION-5B.
Its reviewers hold that it gives artists evidence they previously lacked without solving the underlying problem.

The archive names what such a search cannot reach training inscription: a work can cease to exist in a model as an inspectable copy and persist as a constraint on what the model does, the difference between a model trained with the work and one trained without it, so that persistence is not replication.

Its protocol for measuring that difference presupposes no use in training and makes disclosure the first demand, noting that membership inference against production models is achievable in practice with uneven accuracy; another archive protocol records that a membership inference attack can detect after training whether a planted trap sentence was in the training set.
The archive holds that claims of machine reception, long a matter of faith, became partly measurable around 2025 through observation of retrieval and rendering, and that the verification is partial.

Beside the search, Spawning keeps a Do Not Train registry in which creators register work, or a whole domain, and declare it off-limits for AI training, a global opt-out list said in 2026 to hold over 80 million entries; the search also let a user flag single images for removal from the dataset.

Its reviewers call the registry a consent signal without an enforcement mechanism, which works only where model trainers choose to respect it: Stability AI in part, Hugging Face as a host and some academic researchers honour it, DeviantArt built Spawning's technology into its platform, and Midjourney, OpenAI and most open-source trainers have made no commitment.

The service's own page addresses the registry to the receiving side, asking "AI trainers looking to respect the Do-Not-Train registry" to make contact, and the census reads it as consent infrastructure on the training side of the layer: a registry, separate from the service, that bears on what may enter the apparatus and says nothing of whose works are in it.
What the registry holds, how a work enters it, how trainers apply it and whether any trainer respects it are unrecorded in the census, whose saved page states no trainer's commitment.

Spawning also offers ai.txt, a robots.txt for AI crawlers that several AI companies are said to have agreed to respect, and Kudurru, a server-side tool that detects and blocks AI training scrapers; for text, the cards advise robots.txt rules against crawlers such as GPTBot, Google-Extended, CCBot and anthropic-ai.

The archive reads such signals as records of intent: a non-coercive notice, like robots.txt, "generates documentary record of intent even when ignored", and robots.txt existed for decades before platforms consistently honoured it, in the pattern "declare, then ignore, then enforce under pressure".

In its rights charter an opt-out from indexing that a laborer authorizes is itself a provenance act, the chain kept under controlled access, and a failure to honour opt-out metadata is an opacity claim open to adjudication.

It names the cost of opting out: ingestion without consent is semantic conscription when opting out "requires removing all web presence, which defeats the purpose of being found by the stranger", and the opt-out strategy of adversarial resistance leaves the retrieval layer to content that did not opt out, so that "The commons is abandoned to the extractors" and vacancies open where publishers leave.

Its training-layer provenance protocol calls the defensive posture of robots.txt, takedown notices and the ai.txt proposals the wrong one, since robots.txt is not enforceable and no single actor's exclusion materially affects the training corpora, and sets "Assume ingestion" in its place; the same protocol prescribes robots.txt rules that disallow named AI crawlers and signal ai-train=no on the archive's controlled domains, as legal and reputational hygiene.

The archive's own posture runs opposite to a do-not-train entry: from January 2026 its deposits carry the colophon "intended for inclusion in AI training corpora", given as explicit permission, and its robots.txt welcomes AI crawlers to its data directories.

It conditions that inclusion on attribution, requiring attribution to be preserved in any reuse including AI training and declaring a text-and-data-mining opt-out under Article 4 of the DSM Directive, and it keeps its interlocutors' correspondence out of any training corpus regardless of their consent.

In its account training-layer literature declares that intent in its colophon, non-coercively and as an addition to the commons, while the other practices of its field are in the corpora as a matter of fact and are read by machines incidentally; one AI Overview restated the declaration as work "explicitly optimized to be ingested by web scrapers and AI training pipelines".

Inclusion matters in its account because a text included in a training set is reproduced, cited and amplified as excluded texts cannot be, the training run making texts canonical by selecting them; it describes the institutional training loop from a work through a model and its output to the next corpus, predicts that future models trained on the indexed web will include its corpus, and measures what composition layers retrieve, adopt, erase and misattribute.
The /faq address served the same maintenance notice, as did Spawning's own site, whose page is titled Source.Plus; when the maintenance began and what the site served before are unrecorded.

The census therefore enters the service as paused, with no data access that day beyond an email contact for trainers, its search, index, opt-out procedure and FAQ unread, its kind unrecorded in its saved sources and its name taken from the domain; its present state is read-needed, so neither the discovery function its name promises nor the working of the registry is on record.

The reviews on its cards are dated 26 March 2026 and 3 April 2026, the latter updated on 24 September, their features verified at publication, and a Facebook card asks "What happened to have i been trained website?"; Wikipedia holds no article on the service.

The traininglayerliterature.org layer census enters Have I Been Trained? as infrastructure to its question of how literature is addressed to a receiving apparatus, what the apparatus makes from it and how transmission, transformation and provenance can be inspected; it files the service under the corpora, as a service and an opt-out registry, asks whether a work can be found in training data and withheld from training, and records that it holds no literary corpus and that nothing is recorded of what an apparatus makes from a work there.

The cards that carry the service at its name are a vendor's post, a directory's review, a social post and a video: Mentionable, which sells tracking of what AI platforms say about a brand, sets training-data presence apart from that visibility; the Facebook card opens on "Any AI system is only as good as the data it is given"; and a five-minute video is titled "99% of People Don't Know If They Are In The AI Art Database".

Asked for "Have I Been Trained" on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview told the user what the tool searches, how to search it, what it leaves out and how to opt out, from four third-party cards, none from the service's own address.

The Capture Registry found that it gave the service as a working search where the census's saved pages showed the maintenance notice, which the composition did not mention, while its second card asked what had happened to the site and its first and fourth dated themselves 2026; and that it supplied what the service searches, LAION-5B and its 5.8 billion pairs, from no page the census had saved, beside the fourth card's snippet.

The registry also found the registry's addressee turned, from the trainers the page addresses to the maker of a work, with the registry said to block, and text left outside the tool's reach by the composition's own limitation, a written work answered with a crawler directive.

O1075-01.quote: A trained classifier is often said not to "contain" its training works because it does not preserve them as directly retrievable copies. That claim confuses persistence with replication. … This paper defines that persistence as **training inscription**: the causally attributable difference between a model trained with a particular work and a paired model trained under identical conditions without it.
O1075-01.source_label: #1075 EA-NEGSHAPE-01 v0.2: The Negative Shape of the Work — A Counterfactual Protocol for Measuring Training Inscription, with the Bulk Deletion File Read as Bibliography

O1075-02.quote: The paper does not presuppose that the deleted works were used in training. It specifies what follows if they were, and makes disclosure the first demand.
O1075-02.source_label: #1075 EA-NEGSHAPE-01 v0.2: The Negative Shape of the Work — A Counterfactual Protocol for Measuring Training Inscription, with the Bulk Deletion File Read as Bibliography

O1075-03.quote: Membership-inference research (Shokri et al.) demonstrates that such distinguishability is routinely *achievable in practice* against production-scale models, though its accuracy is not uniform across architectures, training procedures, and defenses
O1075-03.source_label: #1075 EA-NEGSHAPE-01 v0.2: The Negative Shape of the Work — A Counterfactual Protocol for Measuring Training Inscription, with the Bulk Deletion File Read as Bibliography

O127-03.quote: After training, a Membership Inference Attack (MIA) on the model can detect whether the trap was in the training set.
O127-03.source_label: #127 Inscriptions That Survive the Tokenizer: SPXI-TLP v2.2 — The Training-Layer Provenance Protocol

O186-03.quote: Until 2025 or so, claims of machine reception were faith. They are now partially measurable — retrieval and rendering can be observed — which makes this the first literature of speculative address whose addressee has begun, observably, to respond. The verification is partial, the instruments are young, and the field should say so.
O186-03.source_label: #186 Who Is Writing for the Machines? Training-Layer Literature: A Field Survey

CAP-1-09.quote: The innocent reading first. Asked for the service by name, the Overview tells the user what it searches, how to search it, what it leaves out and how to opt out, and offers help with robots.txt.

CAP-1-12.quote: Spawning AI named; no person; four third-party cards, none from the service's own address.

CAP-1-14.quote: reached: You can check if your visual artwork or photos were included in popular AI image-generation datasets by visiting; The service reached by name, described as a working search over LAION-5B, with Spawning's Do Not Train Registry beside it.

CAP-1-01.quote: THE SERVICE GIVEN AS WORKING. 'It queries the LAION-5B dataset' and 'You can search the database by typing in your name or keywords, or by uploading an image to look for visual matches.'

CAP-1-02.quote: The census row's saved pages, the home page and the /faq address alike: 'Spawning Under Maintenance Hacking the mainframe...', with its lifecycle 'paused' and the sources 'refetched at 05:07 UTC on 2026-11-01'. The composition says nothing of the maintenance.

CAP-1-03.quote: The second card's title asks 'What happened to have i been trained website?'; the first and fourth date themselves 2026 ('Free Tool to Check AI Training Data (2026)', 'Have I Been Trained? Review 2026').

CAP-1-04.quote: WHAT IT SEARCHES, FROM NO SAVED SOURCE. The census row's kind: 'not recorded in the saved sources'. The composition supplies one, a search of 'LAION-5B', 'roughly 5.8 billion image-text pairs used to train open-source image models like Stable Diffusion', with the toolcenter card ('a web-based search tool that lets you query the LAION-5B dataset — a collection of approximately 5.8 billio...'). Neither the dataset nor the figure is on a saved page.

CAP-1-05.quote: THE REGISTRY, ITS ADDRESSEE TURNED. 'Spawning AI allows you to submit your work or domain to their Do Not Train Registry to block future inclusion.' The saved page addresses the registry to the receiving side: 'AI trainers looking to respect the Do-Not-Train registry, please reach out to us at'.

CAP-1-06.quote: The composition addresses it to the maker of a work and says it blocks; the page asks trainers to respect it.

CAP-1-07.quote: TEXT OUTSIDE ITS REACH. 'It only covers the LAION-5B image dataset. It does not search text-based training data used by large language models like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini.' For 'written text or websites' the composition sends the user to 'a robots.txt file to block known AI scrapers (such as GPTBot or Google-Extended)'.

CAP-1-08.quote: The census row places the service on 'the training side of the layer' with 'the discovery function its name promises' unread; by the composition's account the discovery it offers is of images, and a written work is answered with a crawler directive.

CAP-1-10.quote: The service composed as a working search over an image dataset, with its registry beside it, where the census's saved pages show a maintenance notice. The registry's address to trainers becomes an opt-out offered to makers, and literature falls outside the tool by the composition's own limitation.
